## Load libraries

```{r}
#| message: false
library("tidyverse")
library("broom")
```

## Load data

The wide file has about 16,600 gene columns, so each line is longer than
the default read buffer. The buffer is increased before reading.

```{r}
#| message: false
Sys.setenv("VROOM_CONNECTION_SIZE" = "5000000")

dat <- read_tsv("../data/03_dat_aug.tsv.gz")
```

## PCA

Genes with zero variance are removed first, otherwise scaling does not work.

```{r}
pca_fit <- dat |>
  select(starts_with("ENSG")) |>
  select(where(~ var(.x) > 0)) |>
  prcomp(scale. = TRUE)
```

## PC1 vs PC2

```{r}
pca_aug <- pca_fit |>
  augment(dat)

pca_condition <- pca_aug |>
  ggplot(aes(x = .fittedPC1, y = .fittedPC2, colour = condition)) +
  geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(x = "PC1", y = "PC2", colour = "Condition",
       title = "PCA coloured by condition") +
  theme_minimal()

pca_condition

ggsave("../results/06_pca_condition.png", pca_condition,
       width = 6, height = 5)
```

The normal samples group together and are separated from the tumors
along PC2. The tumor samples are much more spread out, so the tumors are
more heterogeneous than the normal tissue.

There is a group of tumors with high PC1 values that lies apart from the
rest. It could be a subtype, but we did not look further into it. A few
tumors are close to the normal samples, maybe because those samples contain
a lot of normal tissue.

So tumor vs normal is one of the main things that drives the variation in
the data, which fits with the comparison we did in 05_analysis_1.

```{r}
pca_gender <- pca_aug |>
  ggplot(aes(x = .fittedPC1, y = .fittedPC2, colour = gender)) +
  geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(x = "PC1", y = "PC2", colour = "Gender",
       title = "PCA coloured by gender") +
  theme_minimal()

pca_gender

ggsave("../results/06_pca_gender.png", pca_gender,
       width = 6, height = 5)
```

Male and female samples are mixed together, so sex does not explain much
of the variation. The two grey points are samples where sex is missing.

## Variance explained

```{r}
pca_eigen <- pca_fit |>
  tidy(matrix = "eigenvalues")

pct_pc1 <- pca_eigen |>
  filter(PC == 1) |>
  pull(percent)
pct_pc2 <- pca_eigen |>
  filter(PC == 2) |>
  pull(percent)

pca_variance <- pca_eigen |>
  filter(PC <= 10) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = PC, y = percent)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:10) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = "Principal component",
       y = "Variance explained",
       title = "Variance explained by the first 10 PCs") +
  theme_minimal()

pca_variance

ggsave("../results/06_pca_variance.png", pca_variance,
       width = 6, height = 4)
```

PC1 explains around `r round(100 * pct_pc1)`% of the variance and PC2
around `r round(100 * pct_pc2)`%. The rest is
spread over many components, which is normal for gene expression data.

Dead end: before the CPM normalisation PC1 explained around 36% of the
variance, but most of that came from the differences in sequencing depth
between the samples.
